title: Sabaidee: greeting people and introducing yourself
goal: Greet anyone at any time of day, say your name, ask someone's name, and say where you're from — four sentences you'll use on every first day, anywhere.
bekal: greet people with ສະບາຍດີ
say your name with ຂ້ອຍຊື່…
ask ເຈົ້າຊື່ຫຍັງ
say where you're from with ເປັນຄົນ…
answer with ແມ່ນ and ບໍ່ແມ່ນ

dialogs.title: ບົດສົນທະນາ — In the office lobby, first day
dialogs.intro: Budi has just arrived in Vientiane and meets a coworker. Notice how few words are used — Lao never attaches anything to its verbs, so the sentences stay short.

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ສະບາຍດີ|Sa-baai-dii] [ຂ້ອຍ|Khàwy][ຊື່|sʉ̂ʉ][ບູດີ|Buu-dii] [ເຈົ້າ|Jâo][ຊື່|sʉ̂ʉ][ຫຍັງ|nyǎng]
lines.id: Hello. My name is Budi. What's your name?
lines.literal: well-good. I — name — Budi. you — name — what?

lines.speaker: ບຸນມີ:
lines.text: [ຂ້ອຍ|Khàwy][ຊື່|sʉ̂ʉ][ບຸນມີ|Bun-míi] [ຍິນດີ|Nyín-dii][ທີ່|thìi][ໄດ້|dâi][ຮູ້ຈັກ|hûu-ják]
lines.id: I'm Bounmy. Nice to meet you.
lines.literal: I — name — Bounmy. glad — that — get — know.

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ຍິນດີ|Nyín-dii][ຄື|khʉʉ][ກັນ|kan] [ເຈົ້າ|Jâo][ເປັນ|pen][ຄົນ|khón][ລາວ|Láao][ບໍ່|bàw]
lines.id: Nice to meet you too. Are you Lao?
lines.literal: glad — same — together. you — be — person — Lao — (question)?

lines.speaker: ບຸນມີ:
lines.text: [ແມ່ນ|Mèen][ແລ້ວ|lèeo] [ຂ້ອຍ|Khàwy][ເປັນ|pen][ຄົນ|khón][ວຽງຈັນ|Wíang-jan] [ເຈົ້າ|Jâo][ເດ|dee]
lines.id: Yes. I'm from Vientiane. And you?
lines.literal: right — already. I — be — person — Vientiane. you — how-about?

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ຂ້ອຍ|Khàwy][ບໍ່ແມ່ນ|bàw mèen][ຄົນ|khón][ລາວ|Láao] [ຂ້ອຍ|Khàwy][ເປັນ|pen][ຄົນ|khón][ອິນໂດເນເຊຍ|in-doo-nee-sia]
lines.literal: I — not — person — Lao. I — be — person — Indonesia.

lines.speaker: ບຸນມີ:
lines.text: [ໂອ້|Ôo] [ເຈົ້າ|Jâo][ມາ|maa][ຈາກ|jàak][ໃສ|sǎi]

lines.speaker: ບຸນມີ:
lines.text: [ເຈົ້າ|Jâo][ເວົ້າ|vâo][ພາສາ|phaa-sǎa][ລາວ|Láao][ໄດ້|dâi][ບໍ່|bàw]

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ໄດ້|Dâi][ໜ້ອຍ|nàwy][ໜຶ່ງ|nʉ̀ng] [ຂ້ອຍ|Khàwy][ຫາ|hǎa][ຮຽນ|hían][ຢູ່|yùu]
lines.literal: can — little — one. I — seek — study — (ongoing).

lines.speaker: ບຸນມີ:
lines.text: [ເກັ່ງ|Kèng][ຫຼາຍ|lǎai] [ຂໍ|Khǎw][ໃຫ້|hài][ໂຊກດີ|sôok-dii][ເດີ້|dòe]

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ຂອບໃຈ|Khàwp-jai][ຫຼາຍໆ|lǎai-lǎai] [ພົບ|Phop][ກັນ|kan][ໃໝ່|mài]
lines.id: Thank you very much. See you again.

notes: **ສະບາຍດີ sa-baai-dii is the only greeting you need.** Literally "well-good," it works morning, noon, and night, for both hello and goodbye. Lao has no separate "good morning/good evening" the way English does. One word, every situation.
**ຊື່ sʉ̂ʉ means both "name" AND "to be named."** There's no "is" in between: *ຂ້ອຍຊື່ບູດີ* is literally "I name Budi." Think of the casual English "I'm Budi," just with *ຊື່* in the middle.

**ເປັນ pen means "to be," but only for CATEGORIES.** *ຂ້ອຍເປັນຄົນລາວ* (I'm Lao), *ລາວເປັນອາຈານ* (he's a teacher). To point out identity or sameness, Lao uses a different word — *ແມ່ນ mèen* — and the two can't be swapped. Compare: *ຂ້ອຍເປັນນັກຮຽນ* (I'm a student) versus *ແມ່ນຂ້ອຍ* (it's me).

**ບໍ່ bàw at the END of a sentence turns it into a yes/no question.** *ເຈົ້າເປັນຄົນລາວບໍ່* = "are you Lao?" The same word BEFORE a verb means "not": *ຂ້ອຍບໍ່ໄປ* (I'm not going). Position decides, not sound.

**Answering yes/no questions: repeat the verb.** Lao has no stand-alone "yes" and "no" like English. Asked *ໄປບໍ່* (going?), you answer *ໄປ* (go) or *ບໍ່ໄປ* (not go). Asked *ແມ່ນບໍ່*, you answer *ແມ່ນ* or *ບໍ່ແມ່ນ*.

**ເຈົ້າ jâo does two jobs.** Inside a sentence it means "you." On its own as an answer, it's a polite "yes" — used by men and women alike. ⚠️ This is a big difference from Thai, which splits *ครับ* and *ค่ะ* by the speaker's gender. Lao doesn't.

**ເດີ້ dòe at the end of a sentence softens everything.** Without it, *ໂຊກດີ* sounds like an announcement. With it, it sounds like a friend's good wishes. Use it for kind words, reminders, and goodbyes — but not in every sentence, or it sounds put on.

**ຫຼາຍ lǎai means "much/many" and is used for "very."** It comes after the adjective: *ເກັ່ງຫຼາຍ* (very skilled), *ແພງຫຼາຍ* (very expensive). Doubled as *ຫຼາຍໆ*, it's even stronger: *ຂອບໃຈຫຼາຍໆ* = thank you so very much.

grammars.title: Basic word order: just like English
body: Lao builds sentences as **subject — verb — object**, just like English, and never changes a single letter of the verb. No past forms, no plurals, no agreement of any kind.
after: Question words stay **where the answer goes** instead of jumping to the front as in English. That's why *ເຈົ້າຊື່ຫຍັງ* is built exactly like "you name what?"

grammars.title: ເປັນ, ແມ່ນ, ຢູ່ — three words for one "to be"
body: English uses "to be" for everything. Lao splits that job among three words, and each has its own territory.

after: The negatives: *ບໍ່ເປັນ*, *ບໍ່ແມ່ນ*, *ບໍ່ຢູ່*. The one you'll hear most is **ບໍ່ແມ່ນ** — that's how Lao people say "no, it isn't."
⚠️ *ບໍ່ເປັນຫຍັງ bàw pen nyǎng* (literally "not be what") is a fixed phrase meaning both "it's okay" **and** "you're welcome." Don't take it apart.

blocks.text: One habit worth copying: Lao people greet by **pressing their palms together in front of the chest** — this is called *ນົບ nop*. How high the hands go depends on who you're greeting: chest level for peers, higher for elders and monks. You don't have to do it, but returning it when someone greets you that way is much appreciated.

sections.title: Countries and nationalities: one pattern for all

blocks.text: Lao has no separate word for "Indonesian" or "English." It just puts **ຄົນ *khón*** (person) in front of the country name — "person-Laos" for a Lao.

blocks.text: The word *ຝຣັ່ງ fa-lang* has a long history: it originally meant "French," but in everyday speech it means **any white Westerner**. If you hear it at the market, it's not an insult — just the word people use. Asian visitors rarely get called that; more often they hear the guess *ຄົນໄທບໍ່* (are you Thai?).
